n:
- God offers protection (*refuge;* see {{Psalm 5:11|Psalms 5:11}}; {{Psalm 9:9|9:9}}; {{Psalm 25:20|25:20}}) when justice fails.

- The mountains offer another place of refuge (see {{Psalm 121:1|Psalm 121:1}}).

The psalmist affirms his faith in the righteous God. Even though the world appears hopelessly chaotic, both the godly and the wicked can depend on God’s justice. The godly can depend on him as a refuge and shelter.
The wicked live in the shadows and create gloom for the godly ({{Psalm 82:5|Psalms 82:5}}; {{Psalm 139:11|139:11}}; {{Psalm 143:3|143:3}}; {{Proverbs 4:19|Proverbs 4:19}}).
In the ongoing struggle between those who do evil and those who follow God, the wicked often harm the righteous. This can leave the godly confused and full of questions.
The wicked create a world of darkness (see {{Psalm 82:5|Psalms 82:5}}).

The righteous King rules from heaven, where his throne remains free from human corruption (see {{Psalm 2:4|Psalm 2:4}}). He examines everyone and sees everything that happens on earth (see {{Psalm 14:2-3|Psalm 14:2–3}}).

- *hates*: See {{Psalm 5:4-6|Psalm 5:4–6}}; {{Proverbs 6:16-18|Proverbs 6:16–18}}. 

- Wicked deeds result in destruction and violence ({{Psalm 58:2|Psalms 58:2}}; {{Psalm 73:6|73:6}}; {{Psalm 74:20|74:20}}).
God sent fiery coals and burning sulfur on Sodom and Gomorrah ({{Genesis 19:1-38|Genesis 19}}) as symbols of judgment ({{Psalm 18:8|Psalms 18:8}}; {{Psalm 120:4|120:4}}; {{Psalm 140:10|140:10}}).
The godly are assured of the Lord’s favorable presence when they see his face (see {{Psalm 23:6|Psalm 23:6}}).

Evil becomes so widespread that the godly pray for rescue ({{Isaiah 57:1|Isaiah 57:1}}; {{Micah 7:2|Micah 7:2}}; compare {{Psalm 1:6|Psalms 1:6}}; {{Psalm 37:20|37:20}}; {{Psalm 58:7|58:7}}; {{Psalm 104:35|104:35}}).
This prayer from the community asks the Lord for help against the many evil acts in the world. Because God answers, the godly can face the future with confidence, knowing that God protects them.
The words they say reveal the character of the wicked. They deceive and overpower the godly and arrogantly question the Lord’s purposes.

- The godly can trust the Lord's promises, but not the lies of the wicked ({{Psalm 12:2-4|Psalm 12:2–4}}). 

- *Sevenfold* means entirely or completely.

Those who follow God know that he cares, even when the wicked oppress them. God sees the corrupt and foolish people who praise those who do evil (see {{Psalm 9:19-20|Psalms 9:19–20}}; {{Psalm 14:2-6|14:2–6}}).
*How long?*: Repeating the question four times shows intense worry and deep pain ({{Psalm 79:5|Psalm 79:5}}).
The psalmist’s loud cry for help becomes a confident song of hope.

A feeling of deep sadness and pain can make it hard to see any hope ({{Psalm 6:3|Psalm 6:3}}). Without God’s answer to his prayers ({{Psalm 22:1|Psalm 22:1}}), death seems unavoidable, painful, and slow ({{Psalm 6:6|Psalms 6:6}}; {{Psalm 32:3|32:3}}; {{Psalm 55:4|55:4}}; {{Psalm 61:2|61:2}}; {{Psalm 102:5|102:5}}; {{Psalm 116:3|116:3}}). The psalmist struggles to pray and longs for God's redemption ({{Psalm 25:17-18|Psalms 25:17–18}}; {{Psalm 31:10|31:10}}; {{Psalm 38:8|38:8}}; {{Psalm 39:2|39:2}}).
The psalmist's suffering feels like death ({{Psalm 22:15|Psalms 22:15}}; {{Psalm 55:4|55:4}}; {{Psalm 88:15|88:15}}; {{Psalm 94:17|94:17}}; {{Psalm 116:3|116:3}}).
Only the Lord can provide understanding and comfort. The psalmist hopes for the Lord's justice so his enemies will not celebrate.
The psalmist no longer hears the mockery of his enemies. Instead, he feels joyful because he trusts in the Lord.

Also known as fools, the wicked talk to themselves, think, scheme ({{Psalm 10:4|Psalm 10:4}}, {{Psalm 10:6|6}}, {{Psalm 10:11|11}}), and make claims. However, because they ignore God’s revelation, they lack understanding ({{Psalm 14:1|Psalms 14:1}}; {{Psalm 39:8|39:8}}; {{Psalm 53:1|53:1}}; {{Psalm 74:18|74:18}}, {{Psalm 74:22|22}}).
Paul uses phrases from the Greek translation of this passage in his description of the wickedness of all people ({{Romans 3:10-12|Romans 3:10–12}}).

This wisdom psalm includes elements of lament and prophetic speech. The ideals of {{Psalm 8:1-9|Psalm 8}} clash with foolish human attitudes and sinful actions. Except for verses{{Psalm 14:5-6|5–6}}, this psalm is similar to {{Psalm 53:1-6|Psalm 53}}.

From heaven ({{Psalm 33:13|Psalms 33:13}}; {{Psalm 80:14|80:14}}; {{Psalm 102:19|102:19}}), the Lord sees the wicked, who are clearly evil ({{Psalm 11:3-5|Psalm 11:3–5}}). All humans lack wisdom and do not live in the way God originally intended for them ({{Psalm 10:4-11|Psalm 10:4–11}}; see {{Romans 1:1-3:31|Romans 1–3}}).

The evil live at the expense of others ({{Psalm 27:2|Psalms 27:2}}; {{Psalm 44:11|44:11}}; {{Psalm 53:4|53:4}}; see {{Isaiah 5:8|Isaiah 5:8}}) and have no reverence or knowledge of God ({{Psalm 79:6|Psalm 79:6}}).
Though the wicked perish ({{Psalm 1:5-6|Psalm 1:5–6}}), God is with the righteous.

- The psalmist prays for the renewal of God’s relationship with his people.

- *Jacob* is another name for *Israel* (see {{Genesis 35:9-10|Genesis 35:9–10}}).

- Only those who follow God may be in the Lord’s presence ({{Psalm 5:4|Psalm 5:4}}). As his guests, they experience his hospitality and protection.

- *tent*: In David’s time, God’s sanctuary was a tent (the tabernacle; see {{1 Samuel 21:6|1 Samuel 21:6}}; {{2 Samuel 6:17|2 Samuel 6:17}}; {{2 Samuel 7:6|7:6}}; {{2 Samuel 12:20|12:20}}; {{1 Chronicles 6:32|1 Chronicles 6:32}}).

This wisdom poem contrasts the lifestyle of the righteous with the actions of fools ({{Psalm 14:1-7|Psalm 14}}). The questions in this psalm invite people to examine themselves and not pay attention to problems with the wicked. The question of who dwells in God’s presence leads into a description of godly character qualities (compare {{Psalm 24:3-6|Psalm 24:3–6}}; {{Isaiah 33:14-16|Isaiah 33:14–16}}).

The psalms in this section emphasize integrity and purity ({{Psalm 17:15|Psalms 17:15}}; {{Psalm 18:20-26|18:20–26}}; {{Psalm 19:13-14|19:13–14}}). They describe people as living in God’s presence ({{Psalm 16:9-11|Psalms 16:9–11}}; {{Psalm 17:15|17:15}}) and remaining steadfast ({{Psalm 15:5|15:5}}; {{Psalm 16:8|16:8}}).
The godly speak truthfully and act faithfully in their relationships. Unlike the wicked, they are open and transparent ({{Psalm 12:2-4|Psalm 12:2–4}}).

- The Lord prohibited Israel from charging interest to people in need ({{Exodus 22:25-27|Exodus 22:25–27}}). 

- The assurance of God’s presence keeps the godly from destruction ({{Psalm 16:8|Psalms 16:8}}; {{Psalm 46:5|46:5}}; {{Psalm 125:1|125:1}}). Their situations may temporarily unsettle them, but they ultimately remain strong ({{Psalm 30:6|Psalm 30:6}}; {{Psalm 94:18|94:18}}; {{Psalm 112:6|112:6}}).

The psalmist feels safe because only the Lord offers: 

- security ({{Psalm 16:5-6|Psalm 16:5–6}}),

- guidance ({{Psalm 16:7-8|Psalm 16:7–8}}), and

- the joy of his presence ({{Psalm 16:9-11|Psalm 16:9–11}}).

In this psalm of confidence, the poet quickly transitions from a brief request ({{Psalm 16:1|Psalm 16:1}}) to expressions of deep commitment to God and his people ({{Psalm 16:2-6|Psalm 16:2–6}}). The psalm concludes with confident praise ({{Psalm 16:7-11|Psalm 16:7–11}}).
*I said to the LORD*: The various writers of the psalms pray, lament, and praise the Lord throughout the Psalter (the book of Psalms). The Lord answers them (see {{Psalm 12:5-6|Psalm 12:5–6}}).
The psalmist separates himself from unholy worship, rituals, and words (see {{Psalm 15:3-5|Psalm 15:3–5}}).
The cup of blessing represents how God supplies all the psalmist's needs ({{Psalm 23:5|Psalm 23:5}}; see {{Psalm 116:13|116:13}}; compare {{Psalm 75:8|75:8}}; {{Isaiah 51:17|Isaiah 51:17}}).
The land is God’s gift for his people ({{Deuteronomy 18:8|Deuteronomy 18:8}}).

- God's guidance gives life ({{Psalm 16:11|Psalm 16:11}}; see {{Psalm 5:8|5:8}}; {{Psalm 23:1-3|23:1–3}}; {{Psalm 32:8|32:8}}; {{Psalm 73:24|73:24}}). 

- The psalmist relies on the Lord for strength and joy, feeling God's presence beside him ({{Psalm 16:11|Psalm 16:11}}; see {{Psalm 73:23|73:23}}; {{Psalm 109:31|109:31}}; {{Psalm 110:1|110:1}}, {{Psalm 110:5|5}}; {{Psalm 121:5|121:5}}). 

- Peter quoted {{Psalm 16:8-11|Psalm 16:8–11}} in his sermon on the day of Pentecost ({{Acts 2:25-28|Acts 2:25–28}}).

The psalmist feels confident because he knows that even death cannot separate him from the Lord. He fears separation (see {{Psalm 13:3-4|Psalm 13:3–4}}), but he remains confident that he will see the Lord (see {{Psalm 11:7|11:7}}).
The psalmist shows belief that life goes on after death. The apostles applied this text to the resurrection of Jesus ({{Acts 2:25-33|Acts 2:25–33}}; {{Acts 13:35|13:35}}).

*comes from lips free of deceit*: Deception characterizes the wicked. The righteous reject such deceit as a failure of character and pray for rescue from such people ({{Psalm 5:6|Psalms 5:6}}; {{Psalm 43:1|43:1}}; {{Psalm 120:2|120:2}}). They love honesty, truth, and integrity ({{Psalm 15:2-3|Psalms 15:2–3}}; {{Psalm 24:4|24:4}}; {{Psalm 101:7|101:7}}).
The psalmist asks for God's protection and justice, affirms his own integrity, and prays for the Lord to defeat his strong enemies.

Although he is not perfect, the psalmist dedicates himself to the Lord. He does not want to sin through lies, flattery, or gossip (see {{Psalm 10:7|Psalms 10:7}}; {{Psalm 15:2-3|15:2–3}}; {{Psalm 17:1|17:1}}).
The psalmist declares his innocence ({{Psalm 17:1|Psalm 17:1}}) and commits himself to integrity by being open to God’s examination.
This prayer for God's care continues the request begun in {{Psalm 17:1-2|Psalm 17:1–2}} for redemption from evil.

- *as the apple of Your eye* (literally *as the pupil of your eye*): This metaphor shows God's care and love for the psalmist (see {{Deuteronomy 32:10|Deuteronomy 32:10}}). 

- The shadow of God's wings is a place of his protection from enemies and hardship ({{Psalm 36:7|Psalms 36:7}}; {{Psalm 57:1|57:1}}; {{Psalm 61:4|61:4}}; {{Psalm 63:7|63:7}}; {{Psalm 91:4|91:4}}).

The psalmist prays confidently for the Lord's victory, knowing God is more powerful than the evildoers. The psalmist finds joy in the Lord's inheritance ({{Psalm 16:5|Psalm 16:5}}), whereas the wicked search for joy in this world.
*behold Your face*: The psalmist does not allow temporary concerns raised by adversaries to stand in the way of his experiencing a real and lasting relationship with the Lord.

- The servant of the Lord was given the duty to establish God's kingdom on earth (see {{Psalm 78:70|Psalm 78:70}}; {{Psalm 132:10|132:10}}; {{Psalm 144:10|144:10}}). 

- The Lord rescued David from all his enemies by helping him defeat them (see {{2 Samuel 8:1-14|2 Samuel 8:1–14}}).

This psalm describes a royal story of God rescuing his king. A similar version of this psalm appears in {{2 Samuel 22:1-51|2 Samuel 22:1–51}}. The psalm encourages those who hear the earlier prayers for help in {{Psalm 16:1-11|Psalms 16}} and {{Psalm 17:1-15|17}}. 

The psalmist describes the dramatic nature of God’s rescue in three different ways ({{Psalm 18:7-15|Psalm 18:7–15}}, {{Psalm 18:16-19|16–19}}, {{Psalm 18:30-36|30–36}}). The psalm also offers hope that a future Son of David will completely defeat evil ({{Psalm 18:43-50|Psalm 18:43–50}}; compare {{Psalm 2:1-12|Psalm 2}}).

A shield symbolizes protection, salvation, and victory ({{Psalm 7:10|Psalms 7:10}}; {{Psalm 18:2|18:2}}, {{Psalm 18:30|30}}, {{Psalm 18:35|35}}; {{Psalm 84:11|84:11}}; {{Psalm 91:4|91:4}}; {{Psalm 115:9|115:9}}, {{Psalm 115:10|10}}, {{Psalm 115:11|11}}; {{Psalm 119:114|119:114}}; {{Psalm 144:2|144:2}}). It inspires trust, patience, and confidence in God.
God deserves praise for his greatness and faithfulness ({{Psalm 48:1|Psalms 48:1}}; {{Psalm 96:4|96:4}}; {{Psalm 145:3|145:3}}).

God lives in his sanctuary, the heavenly temple ({{Psalm 102:19|Psalm 102:19}}; see {{Psalm 14:2-3|14:2–3}}). He knows everything and sees every person. He will defend and vindicate those who live in a faithful and righteous way (see {{Psalm 11:3-7|Psalm 11:3–7}}).

The destabilization of the whole earth will be a means of God’s judgment ({{Psalm 77:17-18|Psalm 77:17–18}}; {{Psalm 96:9|96:9}}; {{Psalm 97:4|97:4}}; {{Psalm 99:1|99:1}}; {{Psalm 104:32|104:32}}; {{Isaiah 29:6|Isaiah 29:6}}; {{Micah 1:3-4|Micah 1:3–4}}; {{Nahum 1:2-6|Nahum 1:2–6}}; {{Haggai 2:7|Haggai 2:7}}, {{Haggai 2:21|21}}).

The psalmist describes the Lord coming down from heaven to earth. This moment includes powerful signs such as earthquakes, fire, smoke, darkness, and rain. All creation trembles when God appears.

The psalm shows God as the Divine Warrior (a title that describes God fighting for his people, see {{Psalm 97:2-5|Psalm 97:2–5}}) and as the Judge who rules with justice (see {{Psalm 50:1-6|50:1–6}}).

- *His nostrils … His mouth*: The psalmist compares God to an angry person or a fierce creature (see {{Job 41:12-22|Job 41:12–22}}).

- The frightening images of smoke, flames, and glowing coals show God’s anger against sin.
The Lord rules over all of nature (see {{Psalm 104:2-4|Psalm 104:2–4}}; {{Psalm 148:5-6|148:5–6}}).
*a cherub*: See study notes on 1 Chronicles 28:18; 2 Chronicles 3:10–13.
God loves and delights in the psalmist (see {{Psalm 18:1|Psalm 18:1}}), so he will save him ({{Psalm 37:23|37:23}}; {{Psalm 41:11|41:11}}; {{Psalm 91:14-16|91:14–16}}).

The psalmist states that loyalty brings rewards. He trusts in the Lord (see {{Psalm 16:1|Psalm 16:1}}) and promises to live with integrity (see {{Psalm 1:1-6|Psalms 1}}, {{Psalm 15:1-5|15}}, {{Psalm 24:1-10|24}}; see also {{Psalm 19:12-14|19:12–14}}).

- *kept the ways of the LORD*: The psalmist follows God's instructions faithfully (see {{Psalm 25:8-10|Psalm 25:8–10}}). 

- *have not wickedly departed*: The psalmist avoids foolishness (see {{Psalm 1:1-6|Psalms 1}} and {{Psalm 14:1-7|14}}) and chooses wisdom (see {{Psalm 1:1-6|Psalms 1}} and {{Psalm 15:1-5|15}}).
The faithful God remains true to his character. He loves faithfulness, innocence, and purity, and he hates wickedness (see {{Psalm 1:6|Psalm 1:6}}).

- The pure have clean hands (see {{Psalm 18:20-24|Psalm 18:20–24}}). 

- *to the crooked You show Yourself shrewd*: The Lord understands everyone's character and responds to them fairly.
*light my lamp*: The Lord renews the psalmist's life, helping him overcome the darkness of difficult times (see {{Psalm 112:4|Psalms 112:4}}; {{Psalm 119:105|119:105}}).
*scale a wall*: God helps his servants fight their battles.

- *perfect*: God’s character is full of integrity. He is completely trustworthy (see {{Psalm 18:26|Psalm 18:26}}). 

- God promises to protect his people, and he keeps this promise. 

- Seeking God's protection requires trust and faith. Despite his feelings or external circumstances, the psalmist makes a deep commitment to the Lord. He experiences joy ({{Psalm 5:11|Psalms 5:11}}; {{Psalm 64:10|64:10}}) as he waits for the Lord's rescue ({{Psalm 57:1|Psalm 57:1}}).
The psalmist experiences God’s rescue and provision of victory.
The psalmist’s victories come from the Lord. He completely depends on God.
A wide path represents freedom and safety (see {{Psalm 4:8|Psalms 4:8}}; {{Psalm 119:35|119:35}}).
With help from the Divine Warrior, the psalmist experienced victory over his enemies.
Placing a foot on the necks of the enemy represents total victory (see {{Joshua 10:23-26|Joshua 10:23–26}}).

With God’s help and victory, the psalmist gained success in battle and in ruling the nation. In this way, the psalm reflects the promise about David’s royal line in {{Psalm 2:1-12|Psalm 2}}. 

This psalm also answers some of the earlier prayers for help. The laments in earlier psalms begin to find resolution here.
The psalmist again reflects on the Lord’s victories. God’s amazing rescue and the king’s victory are cause for celebration.
God defends and vindicates his servant. In this way, God fulfills the mission he gave him ({{Psalm 2:1-12|Psalm 2}}; see {{Psalm 47:3|47:3}}; {{Psalm 144:2|144:2}}).
The psalmist's vision of praise *among the nations* inspired Paul in his mission to the Gentiles ({{Romans 15:9|Romans 15:9}}).
God appointed David, his chosen leader, to bring order to God's world (see {{Psalm 2:1-12|Psalm 2}}). Both David and his descendants received this responsibility.

- The *glory of God* refers to the Creator's splendor or visible presence ({{Psalm 113:4|Psalm 113:4}}). 

- *God* (Hebrew *’el*): *El* is an ancient name for God. It shows his power as the Creator.

The created world shows God's wisdom, and the heavens are where God lives ({{Psalm 2:4|Psalm 2:4}}; see {{Psalm 8:1|8:1}}; {{Psalm 57:5|57:5}}; {{Psalm 89:6|89:6}}; {{Psalm 115:3|115:3}}). From heaven, God watches over people ({{Psalm 11:4|Psalms 11:4}}; {{Psalm 14:2|14:2}}; {{Psalm 33:13|33:13}}; {{Psalm 53:2|53:2}}; {{Psalm 80:14|80:14}}; {{Psalm 102:19|102:19}}) and helps his followers ({{Psalm 18:6-8|18:6–8}}, {{Psalm 18:13|13}}; {{Psalm 20:6|20:6}}; {{Psalm 57:3|57:3}}; {{Psalm 76:8|76:8}}; {{Psalm 144:5|144:5}}). 

The heavens remain unaffected by human failures and rebellions (see {{Psalm 2:1-4|Psalm 2:1–4}}). They show God's faithfulness, righteousness ({{Psalm 36:5|Psalms 36:5}}; {{Psalm 50:6|50:6}}; {{Psalm 57:10|57:10}}; {{Psalm 85:11|85:11}}; {{Psalm 89:2|89:2}}, {{Psalm 89:5|5}}; {{Psalm 97:6|97:6}}; {{Psalm 108:4|108:4}}), and wisdom ({{Psalm 136:5|136:5}}; see {{Psalm 119:89-90|119:89–90}}). The heavens reveal the Lord’s glory (see {{Psalm 19:1|Psalm 19:1}}) and prove his presence and work.

God's wisdom is clearly shown in many places:

- It appears in the heavens ({{Psalm 19:1-4|Psalm 19:1–4}}),

- in nature ({{Psalm 19:4-6|Psalm 19:4–6}}),

- in his teachings ({{Psalm 19:7-11|Psalm 19:7–11}}), and

- in the life of the psalmist ({{Psalm 19:12-14|Psalm 19:12–14}})

Like {{Psalm 8:1-9|Psalm 8}}, this hymn uses creation to lead people to reflect on God. It offers a calm moment after the intense prayers and victory songs in earlier psalms.

The psalm begins with creation as a source of wisdom. It then moves to God’s word as the perfect source of wisdom. Finally, it ends with the human need for redemption.

- God’s wisdom does not need to be spoken. Through creation, it is seen, felt, and experienced. Paul applied this text to condemn Israel for its lack of receptivity to Jesus Christ ({{Romans 10:18|Romans 10:18}}).

- The sun is part of God’s creation, but it is not a god, as people of other nations in the ancient Near East commonly believed.

God's instructions to humans show his character and wisdom. His guidance is valuable and enjoyable ({{Psalm 119:103|Psalm 119:103}}). It nurtures the individual ({{Proverbs 16:24|Proverbs 16:24}}; {{Proverbs 24:14|24:14}}) and holds more value than material possessions ({{Psalm 81:13-16|Psalm 81:13–16}}).
The psalmist knows his weaknesses, so he prays to remain faithful and commits himself to the Lord.

- A person who commits deliberate sins does so with a proud and defiant attitude ({{Psalm 86:14|Psalm 86:14}}; {{Psalm 119:21|119:21}}, {{Psalm 119:69|69}}). 

- The *great transgression* is rebellion (see {{Psalm 32:1|Psalm 32:1}}).
*words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart*: The psalmist desires to please God in everything he says and thinks (see {{Luke 6:45|Luke 6:45}}; {{Romans 12:1-2|Romans 12:1–2}}).

- The title *God of Jacob* shows God's long-standing relationship with his people (see {{Psalm 46:7|Psalms 46:7}}, {{Psalm 46:11|11}}; {{Psalm 75:9|75:9}}; {{Psalm 76:6|76:6}}; {{Psalm 81:1|81:1}}, {{Psalm 81:4|4}}; {{Psalm 84:8|84:8}}; {{Psalm 94:7|94:7}}; {{Psalm 114:7|114:7}}; {{Psalm 146:5|146:5}}). 

- *protect you*: See {{Psalm 59:1-2|Psalm 59:1–2}}.
The community prays for the king’s protection and victory.

This royal prayer asks God to give victory to the king ({{Psalm 20:1-5|Psalm 20:1–5}}). It then expresses confidence that God will bring rescue ({{Psalm 20:6-8|20:6–8}}). The psalm ends with the people asking God to answer their prayer ({{Psalm 20:9|20:9}}).

This series of psalms shows a journey from confidence and commitment ({{Psalm 20:1-21:13|Psalms 20–21}}), through anguish and abandonment ({{Psalm 22:1-31|Psalm 22}}), and finally to comfort, insight, and hope ({{Psalm 23:1-24:10|Psalms 23–24}}).
Gifts and burnt offerings show submission to the Lord (compare {{Psalm 40:6|Psalm 40:6}}).
*make all your plans succeed … grant all your petitions*: These requests might be those mentioned in {{Psalm 21:3-6|Psalm 21:3–6}} (compare {{Psalm 27:4|27:4}}).
Troops carried a victory banner to battle. They gathered under it and encouraged each other to act (see {{Isaiah 11:10|Isaiah 11:10}}, {{Isaiah 11:12|12}}).
God chose his anointed king to be ruler (see {{Psalm 2:7|Psalm 2:7}}).
A community member ({{Psalm 20:1-5|Psalm 20:1–5}}) responds with words of assurance and confidence in God's help.
*chariots and … horses*: These were tools used in war (see {{Psalm 33:16-17|Psalms 33:16–17}}; {{Psalm 76:6|76:6}}; {{Psalm 147:10|147:10}}; {{Isaiah 30:16|Isaiah 30:16}}; {{Isaiah 31:1-3|31:1–3}}).
